entries.title: Hanauma Bay Nature Preserve
entries.summary: Protected marine preserve and popular snorkeling bay in East Oʻahu. Advance reservations are required, it is closed Mondays and Tuesdays, and every visitor must watch a short conservation video before going down to the beach.
details: Closed every Monday and Tuesday, plus Christmas Day and New Year's Day. Open Wednesday through Sunday.
Entry from 6:45 a.m. to 1:30 p.m.; all visitors must leave by 4:00 p.m.
Reservations open 48 hours ahead at 7:00 a.m. Hawaiʻi time on the City and County of Honolulu Parks and Recreation website, and often sell out within minutes.

Parking: $3 per vehicle, cash only ($1 for Hawaiʻi residents). A reservation does not guarantee parking.
A mandatory 9-minute conservation video is shown before entry.
The preserve closes temporarily for maintenance at times (for example, sewer-system work in August 2026). Check the official site before you go.

entries.title: Sandy Beach Park
entries.summary: Southeast Oʻahu beach known for a powerful shorebreak, nicknamed "Broke Neck Beach" because waves breaking in shallow water cause serious neck and spinal injuries. Not recommended for children or inexperienced swimmers.
details: Waves break close to shore and can slam people into the sand, even when the surf looks small.
Lifeguards reportedly rescue an average of 2 to 3 swimmers per day.
Lifeguards urge parents with children to choose a different beach.
If you go in at all, talk to the lifeguards about conditions first, and never turn your back on the ocean, even on the sand.

entries.title: Shorebreak and spinal injuries
entries.summary: Waves that break directly onto the shore cause many of Hawaiʻi's neck and back injuries, often in small surf. The average wave height when a spinal cord injury happens is about 3 feet.
details: Small-looking waves can still be dangerous when they break in shallow water.
Ask a lifeguard before entering the water at an unfamiliar beach.
Keep facing the ocean while standing in or near the water.

entries.title: Choose a lifeguard-protected beach
entries.summary: Hawaiʻi's ocean safety agencies advise swimming only at lifeguard-protected beaches and talking to the lifeguards before going in. Conditions change by season: a beach that is calm in summer can be dangerous in winter.
details: Strong currents and rip currents can pull swimmers away from shore; learn how to recognize them and what to do if caught.
Pick a beach that matches your swimming ability, and consider currents, shorebreak and the season.
Each county publishes lifeguarded beaches with daily schedules and current conditions.

entries.title: How close you can get to sea turtles, monk seals, dolphins and whales
entries.summary: Give sea turtles at least 10 feet and Hawaiian monk seals at least 50 feet (150 feet for a mother and pup). Federal law keeps you 50 yards from spinner dolphins and 100 yards from humpback whales.
details: Sea turtles: at least 10 feet (3 m), on land and in the water (guideline).
Hawaiian monk seals: at least 50 feet (15 m); mothers with pups at least 150 feet (about 45 m) (guideline). Stay behind signs or barriers and keep dogs on a leash.
Quick check for 50 feet: if your thumb at arm's length covers the whole seal, you are likely far enough away.
Spinner dolphins: federal law prohibits swimming with, approaching, or staying within 50 yards (46 m).
Humpback whales: federal law prohibits approaching within 100 yards (91 m), including by boat, kayak, drone or swimming.
Other dolphins and small whales: at least 50 yards (guideline).

details: Emergencies, including people in trouble in the water: 911.
Sick, injured, stranded or dead marine mammals or sea turtles: NOAA Marine Wildlife Hotline, (888) 256-9840.

entries.title: Statewide sunscreen law: no oxybenzone or octinoxate
entries.summary: Hawaiʻi state law prohibits sunscreens containing oxybenzone and octinoxate, two chemicals linked to coral reef damage. Some counties go further and require mineral-only sunscreen.
details: Check the label: avoid oxybenzone and octinoxate anywhere in Hawaiʻi.
Maui County and Hawaiʻi County have stricter mineral-only rules (see their entries).
Mineral sunscreens use zinc oxide or titanium dioxide.

details: Allowed: mineral sunscreens with zinc oxide or titanium dioxide as the active ingredients.

entries.title: Lodging tax (TAT) rose to 11% in 2026: the "green fee"
entries.summary: Starting January 1, 2026, Hawaiʻi's state Transient Accommodations Tax rose 0.75 percentage points to 11% under Act 96, the "green fee." It applies to overnight stays at hotels and vacation rentals, including by Hawaiʻi residents, and now to cruise ship passengers.
details: Gov. Josh Green described the cost as about $3 extra for every $400 spent on lodging.
The added revenue, about $100 million a year, is split among natural resource protection, climate and disaster resilience, and visitor experience.
Each county adds its own 3% lodging tax, for a combined 14% TAT. With general excise tax passed on (up to 4.712%), total lodging taxes can reach about 18.7% of the room rate.

entries.title: Which Hawaiʻi attractions need reservations (by island)
entries.summary: Several top sites require advance booking for visitors: Hanauma Bay, Diamond Head and the USS Arizona Memorial on Oʻahu; Haleakalā sunrise, Waiʻānapanapa and ʻĪao Valley on Maui; Hāʻena State Park and Kīlauea Point on Kauaʻi. Maui: Haleakalā sunrise (60 days and 2 days ahead at 7 a.m.), Waiʻānapanapa (30 days ahead at midnight), ʻĪao Valley (up to 30 days ahead).

entries.title: Taking sand, rocks or coral from beaches is illegal
entries.summary: Hawaiʻi law (HRS 205A-44) prohibits taking sand, dead coral or coral rubble, rocks, soil or other beach deposits from the shoreline. Shells, driftwood, beach glass and seaweed are exempt, as is sand accidentally carried off on your body or gear.
details: The law covers sand, dead coral, coral rubble, rocks, soil and other beach or marine deposits.
Allowed: driftwood, shells, beach glass, glass floats and seaweed; small amounts stuck to your body, clothes, toys or bags.
Other exceptions cover permitted traditional cultural practices, government maintenance and emergencies.
Leave lava rocks and plants where they are, too: local etiquette and many park rules ask visitors not to remove them.

entries.title: Hawaiʻi visitor etiquette: lei, homes, rocks and driving
entries.summary: Accept a lei by lowering your head and never throw one away; take off your shoes before entering a home; don't stack rocks; and drive patiently without honking. Touching or harming endangered or threatened species is a felony under state law.
details: Lei: lower your head so the giver can place it on you, don't take it from their hands, and don't toss it in the trash; it carries cultural significance.
Homes: remove your shoes before entering.
Rocks: don't stack them. Rock stacking isn't a traditional practice, and rocks were used for ahu (altars and trail markers).
Driving: highways max out at 60 mph and speeding fines start at $100; locals rarely honk, pull over for others on narrow roads and one-lane bridges, and a wave or shaka says thanks.
Bicycles: don't ride on sidewalks in business districts such as Waikīkī and downtown Honolulu.
Words: residents of Hawaiʻi are kamaʻāina; not every resident is Native Hawaiian (kanaka maoli).
Don't stand on reefs, slippery ocean-side rock ledges or near blowholes.

entries.title: General excise tax (GET): Hawaiʻi's version of sales tax
entries.summary: Hawaiʻi has no sales tax; it has a general excise tax of 4% plus a 0.5% county surcharge, 4.5% in all four counties. Businesses may pass on up to 4.712% to customers, which is why receipts often show that number.

entries.title: Kalākaua Avenue, Waikīkī's main street
entries.summary: Yes, Kalākaua Avenue is Waikīkī's main oceanfront street. It was first called Waikiki Road and was renamed in the early 1900s for King David Kalākaua (reigned 1874 to 1891), the last king of the Hawaiian Kingdom, known as the Merrie Monarch.
details: Route: about 4.4 km (2.7 miles), from Kapiʻolani Park near Diamond Head, past the Honolulu Zoo and Waikīkī's beaches and hotels, across the Ala Wai Canal, to South Beretania Street in McCully.
Name: originally Waikiki Road. Sources differ on the year it was renamed for King Kalākaua (1905 or 1908).
King Kalākaua (1836 to 1891) championed Hawaiian music, hula and culture, which helped spark the first Hawaiian Renaissance. The Merrie Monarch Festival in Hilo is named for him.
Landmarks along it include the Moana Hotel (1901, now the Moana Surfrider), the Royal Hawaiian Hotel (1927), Kapiʻolani Park and the Honolulu Zoo, with Fort DeRussy nearby.
In the 1990s the city spent more than $100 million over about ten years on new sidewalks, landscaping, historic-style lighting and plazas; the Waikiki Historic Trail was designed in 1994.
Nearby streets are named for Hawaiian royalty and notable figures too, such as Kaʻiulani Avenue (Princess Kaʻiulani) and Duke's Lane (Duke Kahanamoku).

entries.title: Oʻahu hikes from easiest to hardest
entries.summary: Easiest: Mānoa Falls (1.6 miles round trip through rainforest). Easy to moderate: Lanikai Pillbox (1 mile, steep start), Diamond Head (reservation needed for visitors) and Makapuʻu Lighthouse (2 miles, 500 feet). Longer but flat: Kaʻena Point. Hardest: Koko Crater Stairs (1,048 steps, about 1,200 feet straight up). Haʻikū Stairs is illegal and being removed.
details: Easy: Mānoa Falls Trail, 1.6 miles round trip, about an hour, rainforest to a 150-foot waterfall. Muddy and slippery.
Moderate, short: Lanikai Pillbox (Kaʻiwa Ridge), 1 mile round trip, steep and gravelly at the start, no shade, ocean views of the Mokulua islands.
Moderate: Diamond Head State Monument, Honolulu's classic crater hike. Non-residents must reserve ahead.
Moderate: Makapuʻu Point Lighthouse Trail, 2 miles round trip, 500 feet of gain, hot and exposed, whale watching November to May.
Moderate, long and flat: Kaʻena Point, 2.5 miles each way along the coast; check road access closures first.
Strenuous: Koko Crater Stairs, 1,048 old railway ties, about 1,200 feet of gain in under a mile, no shade.
Off-limits: Haʻikū Stairs (Stairway to Heaven) has been illegal to climb since 1987 and the city began removing it in 2024. Trespassers are cited and arrested.
For every trail: start early, carry plenty of water, wear sun protection, stay on the trail, and pack out your trash.

entries.title: Mānoa Falls Trail
entries.summary: One of Oʻahu's easiest hikes: 1.6 miles round trip (about an hour) through Mānoa Valley rainforest to a roughly 150-foot waterfall, near Lyon Arboretum above Honolulu. Expect mud and slippery rocks; don't swim in the pool.
details: Difficulty: easy, good for beginners.
Length: 1.6 miles round trip, about 1 hour.
Trail is rocky and often muddy and slippery; wear sturdy shoes, not slippers.
Don't swim or wade: the Hawaiʻi Department of Health discourages it because of leptospirosis, and signs warn of landslides and flash floods.
Parking: a paid private lot at the end of Mānoa Road (fees have been reported between $5 and $7), or free street parking lower in the neighborhood. Confirm current rates on arrival.

entries.title: Makapuʻu Point Lighthouse Trail
entries.summary: A 2-mile round-trip trail (about 500 feet of climbing) on Oʻahu's southeast tip with views of the lighthouse and the windward coast. Rated moderate by the state; hot, sunny and exposed. Best for whale watching November through May.
details: Length: 2.0 miles round trip; allow about 2 hours.
Elevation gain: 500 feet. State rating: moderate.
Hot, dry and exposed with no shade; very windy at the top. Bring a hat, sunscreen and plenty of water.
Humpback whale season: November through May; binoculars help.
Parking lot off Kalanianaʻole Highway (Route 72) in Kaiwi State Scenic Shoreline.
The lighthouse itself is off-limits. Stay on the trail and pack out trash.
Notice (Oct. 23, 2026): the upper Makapuʻu viewing area is closed for repairs October 21 to November 4, 2026, and all day on weekends and holidays; the Lighthouse Trail itself stays open.

entries.title: Lanikai Pillbox Trail (Kaʻiwa Ridge)
entries.summary: A short but steep 1-mile round-trip ridge hike in Kailua to old military pillboxes with famous views over Lanikai and the Mokulua islands. Free, no shade, and parking in Lanikai is very limited, so park at Kailua Beach Park and walk.
details: Difficulty: moderate. Length: about 1 mile round trip.
Trailhead: Kaelepulu Drive in Lanikai, across from Mid-Pacific Country Club; a narrow signed path between two fences.
Parking: very limited in the neighborhood and cars get towed; park at Kailua Beach Park and walk.
No shade; go early. Gravel sections are slippery, especially going down and after rain.
Free.

entries.title: Koko Crater Stairs (Koko Head)
entries.summary: Oʻahu's famous stair workout: 1,048 old railway ties straight up Koko Crater, about 1,200 feet of climbing in roughly 1.6 miles round trip. Strenuous, with no shade. Free parking at Koko Head District Park in Hawaiʻi Kai.
details: Difficulty: strenuous, nearly vertical with no switchbacks.
1,048 steps (ties from a World War II military tramway); summit at about 1,208 feet.
Time: 45 to 60 minutes round trip for first-timers.
Halfway up, a narrow section crosses a gap like a bridge; a bypass path on the right rejoins the trail.
No shade at all; go early or late and carry water.
Parking: free lot at Koko Head District Park, 423 Portlock Road (lot open 4 a.m. to 11 p.m.).
Free.

entries.title: Kaʻena Point Trail
entries.summary: A flat coastal walk, 2.5 miles each way, to Oʻahu's wild western tip, a protected Natural Area Reserve with nesting seabirds. Rated moderate for heat, wind and eroded sections. Check closures first: storm damage has restricted vehicle access.
details: Length: 2.5 miles one way from either the Waiʻanae (Keawaʻula) or Mokulēʻia side; return the same way. Allow 1 to 3 hours.
Mostly flat on an old railroad bed and dirt road that has fully eroded in places.
Sunny, hot and windy; bring sun protection and plenty of water.
Natural Area Reserve rules: no dogs (service animals only), no drones or fires, stay on paths and watch for nesting seabirds.
Stay away from the wave-exposed coast unless you know hazardous ocean conditions. Whales pass offshore in winter.
Recent DLNR notice: vehicle access in Kaʻena Point State Park was restricted because of storm damage, and the Keawaʻula Trail was closed. Check park notices before going.

entries.title: Haʻikū Stairs (Stairway to Heaven) is illegal and being removed
entries.summary: Climbing Oʻahu's Haʻikū Stairs has been illegal since 1987. The city voted in 2021 to remove them and began removal in 2024. Police cite and arrest trespassers. Choose a legal trail instead.
details: The area is a closed, dangerous construction and natural area; officials cite safety, trespassing, neighborhood impacts and city liability.
In April 2024 alone, police issued dozens of citations and several arrests for trespassing at the stairs.
Legal alternatives with big views: Lanikai Pillbox, Makapuʻu Lighthouse, Koko Crater Stairs or Diamond Head.

entries.title: Lifeguarded beaches on Oʻahu
entries.summary: Most Oʻahu lifeguard towers are staffed daily from 8 a.m. to 6:30 p.m., at beaches on every shore, from Ala Moana and Waikīkī to Waimea Bay and Mākaha. Bellows and Depot's are weekends only.
details: South Shore: Ala Moana Beach Park, Magic Island lagoon, Waikīkī (Duke's, Kūhiō, Queen's and Kapiʻolani Park towers), Sans Souci, Hanauma Bay, Sandy Beach.

Windward: Makapuʻu Beach, Waimānalo Beach, Waimānalo Bay, Bellows Field Beach (weekends only), Kailua Beach, Kualoa Regional Park (daily Memorial Day to Labor Day; weekends and holidays the rest of the year).
North Shore: Sunset Beach, ʻEhukai Beach, Ke Waena Beach, Chun's Reef, Waimea Bay, Laniākea Beach, Haleʻiwa Aliʻi Beach Park.
Leeward (Waiʻanae): Keawaʻula Beach, Mākaha Beach, Māʻili Beach, Depot's Beach (weekends and holidays only), Nānākuli Beach, Pōkaʻī Bay.
Hours: daily 8:00 a.m. to 6:30 p.m. unless noted. If no lifeguard is in the tower, call 911 in an emergency.
Check current hazard ratings for any beach at Hawaii Beach Safety before you go in.

West Maui: D.T. Fleming Beach Park, Hanakaʻōʻō Beach Park.

entries.title: Box jellyfish: when they show up and what to do
entries.summary: Box jellyfish tend to wash in about 8 to 10 days after each full moon, mostly on south- and west-facing (leeward) shores such as Waikīkī, Ala Moana and Salt Pond on Kauaʻi. Lifeguards post warning signs on those days.

Where: mostly leeward, south- and west-facing beaches. Examples where warning signs have been posted include Waikīkī and Ala Moana on Oʻahu and Salt Pond Beach Park on Kauaʻi.
Before you swim: look for yellow box jellyfish signs and ask the lifeguard.
If you are stung: get out of the water, tell a lifeguard, and call 911 if the person has trouble breathing, chest pain or a strong allergic reaction.

entries.title: Caught in a rip current: what to do
entries.summary: A rip current pulls you away from shore, not under. Stay calm and float, swim parallel to the shore to get out of it, and wave your arms for a lifeguard. Never swim in after someone yourself.
details: Float and stay calm. Fighting the current wears you out.
Swim parallel to the shore, then angle back in with the waves.
Wave your arms and call out so a lifeguard or people on the beach can see you.
Helping someone else: alert a lifeguard, throw them something that floats and call 911. Do not go in after them; many rip current deaths are would-be rescuers.
Best protection: swim at a beach with a lifeguard and ask about currents before going in.

entries.title: Flash floods and stream crossings
entries.summary: Flash floods have killed more people in Hawaiʻi than high winds or hurricanes, often people crossing flooded streams. If it is raining hard or a Flood Watch or warning is out, stay out of streams and off flooded roads: Turn Around, Don't Drown.
details: Many flash flood deaths in Hawaiʻi happened to people who crossed or fell into flooded streams.
Water can rise fast even if it is not raining where you are; the rain may be falling up in the mountains.
Do not cross a stream that is rising, muddy or fast. Wait for it to go down.
Never drive through a flooded road.
Flash floods can happen any month but are most common October through April.
Check live alerts on Ask Hawaiʻi or the National Weather Service Honolulu office before a hike.

entries.title: Swimming in streams, ponds and waterfalls: leptospirosis
entries.summary: Hawaiʻi's freshwater streams, ponds and waterfall pools can carry leptospirosis, a bacteria spread by animal urine. The state Health Department advises not swimming or wading in them, especially with cuts, and not putting your head under.
details: You can get it by swimming or wading in fresh water, or touching wet soil or plants contaminated by animal urine.
Risk is higher with open cuts or sores, and if your head goes under (eyes, nose, mouth).
Do not drink stream or pond water unless it has been boiled or treated.
Illness can start 2 days to 4 weeks after exposure, with fever, headache, chills and muscle aches.
If you get sick after freshwater exposure, see a doctor and mention it. It is treated with antibiotics.
Ocean water is not the concern here; this is about fresh water.

entries.title: Warning sirens and the monthly test
entries.summary: Hawaiʻi tests its outdoor warning sirens on the first working day of each month at 11:45 a.m. with a one-minute steady tone. If sirens sound at any other time, treat it as real and turn on local radio, TV or check your phone for alerts.
details: Test: first working day of the month, 11:45 a.m. HST, about one minute, steady tone. No drill goes with it.
Any other time: a siren means an emergency such as a tsunami or other hazard. Get official instructions right away.
Where to get instructions: local radio and TV, and Wireless Emergency Alerts on your phone.

entries.title: Taking fruit, flowers and plants home: airport agriculture inspection
entries.summary: Before flying from Hawaiʻi to the mainland, all food, plants and flowers must go through USDA agriculture inspection at the airport. Fresh pineapple, coconut, coffee and most lei are fine; most other fresh fruit, berries, soil and plants in soil are not.
details: Present all food, plants and other agricultural items at the airport inspection before you check in.
Allowed after inspection: fresh pineapple, coconut, coffee (roasted or green), commercially canned, dried or frozen foods, white potatoes.
Allowed only if commercially treated and boxed with a USDA stamp: papaya, banana, lychee, longan, rambutan, dragon fruit, starfruit, sweet potato and a few others.
Fresh flowers and most lei are allowed, except jade vine, Mauna Loa flowers and citrus parts.
Not allowed: most fresh fruits and vegetables, berries of any kind (including fresh coffee berries), plants in soil, soil, cactus, sugarcane, live insects and snails.
Allowed by USDA: seashells (not land snail shells), driftwood, seed lei. Note that taking sand and rocks from Hawaiʻi beaches is limited by state law; see the sand rule.

entries.title: Rapid ʻŌhiʻa Death: clean your shoes when hiking
entries.summary: A fungus called Rapid ʻŌhiʻa Death is killing ʻōhiʻa, Hawaiʻi's most important native forest tree. Clean mud off shoes and gear before and after hiking, and do not move ʻōhiʻa wood, leaves or flowers between islands.
details: Brush off dirt and mud from shoes, gear and clothes before and after entering a forest, then spray soles with 70% rubbing alcohol.
Wash mud off vehicle tires after driving on dirt roads.
Do not injure ʻōhiʻa trees, and do not move ʻōhiʻa wood or parts.
Do not take ʻōhiʻa lei, flowers or wood from Hawaiʻi Island to other islands.
The fungus has been confirmed on Hawaiʻi Island and Kauaʻi, with detections on Oʻahu and Maui as well.
Many trailheads have boot brush stations; use them.

entries.title: Hawaiian words you will hear
entries.summary: A few words go a long way: aloha (hello, goodbye, love), mahalo (thank you), mauka (toward the mountains), makai (toward the ocean), keiki (child), ʻohana (family), pau (finished), kapu (forbidden, keep out) and mālama (take care of).
details: Aloha: hello, goodbye, love.
Mahalo: thank you. Mahalo nui: thank you very much.
Mauka: toward the mountains. Makai: toward the ocean. Locals give directions this way.
Keiki: child or children.
ʻOhana: family.
Pau: finished, done.
Kapu: forbidden, sacred, keep out. A kapu sign means stay off.
Mālama: take care of, protect, as in mālama ʻāina (care for the land).
Kuleana: responsibility.
Honu: green sea turtle.
Lānai: porch or balcony (the island is spelled Lānaʻi).
Kamaʻāina: local resident; you will see kamaʻāina discounts.
The ʻokina (ʻ) and kahakō (the line over a vowel) change pronunciation and meaning, so Hawaiʻi and Oʻahu are spelled with them.

entries.title: Hawaiʻi time zone (no daylight saving)
entries.summary: Hawaiʻi uses Hawaiʻi-Aleutian Standard Time (UTC minus 10) all year and does not switch for daylight saving time. That puts it 2 hours behind the U.S. West Coast in winter and 3 hours behind in summer.
details: UTC minus 10 hours, all year.
No daylight saving time, so the gap with the mainland changes in March and November.

details: Rush hour: roughly 6 to 8:30 a.m. and 3 to 6:30 p.m. on weekdays. Add 30 to 60 minutes to trips on H-1.
H-1 eastbound (toward town) HOV, 2 or more people: weekdays 5:30 to 9 a.m.
H-1 Zipper Lane eastbound, 2 or more people: weekdays 5:30 to 9 a.m., from Managers Drive (Waipahu) to the Keʻehi Interchange.
H-1 westbound HOV, 2 or more people: weekdays 3 to 7 p.m.
H-2 HOV: southbound 5:30 to 9 a.m., northbound 3:30 to 6 p.m.
Contraflow lanes: Kalanianaʻole Highway westbound 5 to 8 a.m.; Kahekili Highway southbound 4:30 to 8:30 a.m.; Farrington Highway westbound 3:30 to 6:30 p.m.
Lanes don't run on most holidays; HDOT posts exceptions.

entries.title: Aloha Festivals (September, with the Waikīkī Hoʻolauleʻa and Floral Parade)
entries.summary: Hawaiʻi's biggest Hawaiian cultural celebration runs every September. The two big public days are the Waikīkī Hoʻolauleʻa, a street party on Kalākaua Avenue with food, music and hula, and the Floral Parade. In 2026: Hoʻolauleʻa Sept. 19, Floral Parade Sept. 26.
details: Held every September; 2026 was its 80th year.
2026 dates: Royal Court Investiture and Opening Ceremony Sept. 5; Waikīkī Hoʻolauleʻa Sept. 19; Floral Parade Sept. 26.
The Hoʻolauleʻa closes part of Kalākaua Avenue in Waikīkī for an evening block party with food vendors, music stages and hula.
The Floral Parade features pāʻū riders on horseback representing each island, floats and marching bands.
Check alohafestivals.com each summer for that year's dates, times and road closures.

entries.title: Honolulu Festival (March)
entries.summary: A Pacific Rim cultural festival each March with performances at the Hawaiʻi Convention Center and Waikīkī stages, a free Grand Parade on Kalākaua Avenue and Nagaoka fireworks off Waikīkī. The 2027 festival is March 5 to 7.
details: Usually a weekend in March. 2027: March 5 to 7 (Friday to Sunday).
Main venue: Hawaiʻi Convention Center (the Exhibition Hall has a small admission fee; in 2026 it was $10 at the door for adults, children under 18 free).
Free stages around Waikīkī and Ala Moana Center.
Grand Parade on Kalākaua Avenue and the Nagaoka fireworks show over Waikīkī, both free (both were canceled for weather in 2026).
Performers come from Japan, the Philippines, Korea, Taiwan, Tahiti and across the Pacific.

entries.title: Pan-Pacific Festival (June, Waikīkī)
entries.summary: A free three-day festival in Waikīkī each June celebrating Hawaiʻi's cultural ties with Japan and the Pacific. It opens with a Hoʻolauleʻa street party on Kalākaua Avenue and ends with a parade. In 2026 it ran June 12 to 14.
details: Usually the second weekend of June.
Opening night Hoʻolauleʻa closes Kalākaua Avenue between Seaside and Uluniu avenues.
Performances at Ala Moana Center Stage and International Market Place, plus the Pan-Pacific Hula Festival at the Kūhiō Beach hula mound.

entries.title: Merrie Monarch Festival (hula, Hilo, the week after Easter)

entries.title: The Eddie (Eddie Aikau Big Wave Invitational, Waimea Bay)
entries.summary: The most famous big-wave contest in the world, held at Waimea Bay only when waves are big enough: consistent 20-foot-plus Hawaiian-scale surf (about 40-foot faces) for a full day. The waiting period runs from early December to early March, and it has run only 11 times.
details: Waiting period: roughly early December to early March each winter.
It only runs on a day with consistent 20 to 25 foot Hawaiian-scale surf (about 40 to 50 foot faces) all day.
It has run 11 times in 49 years as of the 2025-26 season; it did not run in 2025-26.
When it's called, huge crowds head to Waimea and traffic on Kamehameha Highway backs up for miles. Go very early or take the bus.
It honors Eddie Aikau, Waimea Bay's first lifeguard, who was lost at sea in 1978 while seeking help for the Hōkūleʻa crew.

entries.title: Lunch wagons and plate lunch: how they work
entries.summary: Lunch wagons (food trucks) are a big part of eating in Hawaiʻi. The classic order is a plate lunch: a main dish with two scoops of rice and a scoop of macaroni salad. Many trucks open around late morning, close in the afternoon or when they sell out, and some take cash only.
details: Plate lunch: a main (garlic shrimp, huli chicken, kalua pig, teriyaki beef, chicken katsu, fish) with two scoops of white rice and mac salad.
Lines are longest around the noon hour; going a little before or after helps.
Many trucks take cards now, but some are cash only. Carry some cash.
Many trucks park in the same lot every day; some move around and post their spot online each morning.
Clusters of trucks: Kahuku and Haleʻiwa on Oʻahu's North Shore, Kewalo Basin in Kakaʻako, Kahului and Kīhei on Maui, Kapaʻa on Kauaʻi, and Kailua-Kona on Hawaiʻi Island.
Eat where you're allowed and take your trash with you; many beach parks have no trash service after hours.
Hours and parking spots change often, and trucks can close early when they sell out. Check the truck's Instagram, Facebook or Google listing the day you go.

entries.title: How many botanical gardens are on Oʻahu?
entries.summary: Oʻahu has eight major public gardens. The City runs five Honolulu Botanical Gardens: Foster, Hoʻomaluhia, Koko Crater, Liliʻuokalani and Wahiawā. The other three are the University of Hawaiʻi's Lyon Arboretum in Mānoa, Waimea Valley on the North Shore and Moanalua Gardens, home of the Hitachi Tree.
details: City gardens (Honolulu Botanical Gardens): Foster (downtown, 14 acres), Hoʻomaluhia (Kāneʻohe, about 400 acres), Koko Crater (Hawaiʻi Kai, dryland plants inside a crater), Liliʻuokalani (Nuʻuanu, native plants and a waterfall) and Wahiawā (Central Oʻahu, 27-acre forested ravine).
Lyon Arboretum: University of Hawaiʻi rainforest garden at the back of Mānoa Valley; free, weekdays.
Waimea Valley: North Shore valley garden with a waterfall at the end of the path.
Moanalua Gardens: private park near Moanalua with the famous Hitachi monkeypod tree; small admission fee.
Free: Hoʻomaluhia, Koko Crater and Lyon Arboretum (donation suggested). Foster charges $5 for adults ($3 Hawaiʻi residents).

entries.title: Foster Botanical Garden (downtown Honolulu)

details: Address: 180 N. Vineyard Blvd., Honolulu (near Chinatown).
Hours: 9 a.m. to 4 p.m.; last admission 3:30 p.m. Closed Christmas and New Year's Day.
Admission: adults $5, Hawaiʻi residents $3, children 6 to 12 $1, under 5 free; annual family pass $25.
Free docent tours at 10:30 a.m. Mondays, Wednesdays, Fridays and Saturdays (Thursdays added in 2026), about 90 minutes. Reservations recommended: 808-768-7135.
14 acres: exceptional trees, orchids, palms and cycads, and an outdoor butterfly habitat.

entries.title: Hoʻomaluhia Botanical Garden (Kāneʻohe)
entries.summary: A free, 400-acre garden below the Koʻolau cliffs in Kāneʻohe, with a 32-acre lake and some of the most photographed mountain views on Oʻahu. Open 9 a.m. to 4 p.m., closed Thursdays. Weekend camping and free catch-and-release fishing by reservation.
details: Address: 45-680 Luluku Road, Kāneʻohe. Phone 808-768-8942.
Hours: 9 a.m. to 4 p.m.; closed Thursdays, Christmas and New Year's Day. Last car in at 3:30 p.m.
Admission: free.
You can drive through the garden; park at pull-offs for the views. Please don't stop in the road.
Free catch-and-release fishing: Wednesdays and Saturdays, 10 a.m. to noon and 1 to 3 p.m., by online reservation (opens two weeks ahead); bamboo poles loaned.
Weekend camping: 28 sites, $32 per site Friday to Monday, reserved online at pros.hnl.info (opens Fridays at 5 p.m., two weeks ahead).

entries.title: Koko Crater Botanical Garden (Hawaiʻi Kai)
entries.summary: A free garden inside Koko Crater with rare and endangered dryland plants, cactus and a famous plumeria grove. A 2-mile mostly flat loop trail with little shade, so go early or late in the day.
details: Inside Koko Crater near Hawaiʻi Kai, next to the Koko Crater Stables; unpaved parking lot at the gate.
Free admission; open daylight hours (closed Christmas and New Year's Day).
2-mile loop, mostly flat and dry; plan up to a couple of hours.
Highlights: the plumeria grove (best when blooming in late spring and summer), Hawaiian and Madagascar dryland plants, cactus and succulents.
Very little shade and no water; bring water, hat and sunscreen. Lock your car and keep valuables out of sight.

entries.title: Liliʻuokalani and Wahiawā Botanical Gardens (smaller city gardens)
entries.summary: Two quieter city gardens: Liliʻuokalani Botanical Garden in Nuʻuanu, once Queen Liliʻuokalani's favorite picnic spot, with native plants and a waterfall; and Wahiawā Botanical Garden, a 27-acre forested ravine in cool Central Oʻahu.
details: Liliʻuokalani Botanical Garden: just above Foster Garden across the freeway; native Hawaiian plants, a waterfall on Nuʻuanu Stream, and history as the Queen's picnic grounds.
Wahiawā Botanical Garden: 27 acres in a forested ravine in Wahiawā, first planted as an experimental arboretum in the 1920s; plants that like cool, wet uplands.
Both are free, small and good for a short walk. Check the City's botanical gardens page for current hours.

entries.title: Waimea Valley (North Shore)
entries.summary: A culturally important valley across from Waimea Bay with a botanical garden along a paved path that ends at Waimea Falls. Adults $26, Hawaiʻi residents and military $10. Open Tuesday to Sunday 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. (daily in summer and December).
details: Across Kamehameha Highway from Waimea Bay. Phone 808-638-7766.
Hours: Tuesday to Sunday, 9 a.m. to 4 p.m., closed Mondays. Daily in summer (9 to 5 in 2026) and Dec. 1 to 30. Closed Thanksgiving and Christmas.
Admission: adults $26, seniors 62+ and students $20, children 4 to 12 $18. Kamaʻāina and military with ID: adults $10, seniors and students $8, kids $6.

The valley is managed by Hiʻipaka, a Hawaiian nonprofit, and has archaeological sites and cultural programs.

entries.title: Kauaʻi gardens: Allerton, McBryde, Limahuli and Na ʻĀina Kai

details: Allerton Garden (Lāwaʻi Valley, South Shore): guided tours only, about 2.5 hours, reservations required, about $60 per person. Famous for its giant Moreton Bay fig roots.
McBryde Garden (next to Allerton): self-guided, about $35.
Limahuli Garden (North Shore, near Hāʻena): self-guided trail through a valley of native and Polynesian-introduced plants.
Na ʻĀina Kai Botanical Gardens (near Kīlauea): guided tours of 1.5 to 5 hours, reservations required.

entries.title: Maui gardens: Maui Nui, Kula, Garden of Eden and Kahanu

details: Maui Nui Botanical Gardens: 150 Kanaloa Ave., Kahului, across from War Memorial Stadium. Tuesday to Saturday, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. $10 general; free for kamaʻāina and kids under 12. Focus on native Maui Nui plants.

entries.title: Nēnē, the Hawaiian goose (state bird)
entries.summary: The nēnē is Hawaiʻi's state bird and is found nowhere else on Earth. It nearly vanished, down to about 30 wild birds around 1950, and has recovered to roughly 3,000 thanks to protection. Never feed nēnē, and drive slowly where signs warn of them.
details: Only in Hawaiʻi; descended from geese that arrived long ago and adapted to land, with less webbing on their feet for walking on lava.
Down to about 30 in the wild around 1950; about 3,000 statewide today. Protected under the Endangered Species Act since 1967 and later reclassified from endangered to threatened.
Where to see them: Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park (about 250 there), Haleakalā, and Kauaʻi, including golf courses and grassy areas.
Don't feed them. Fed birds come to roads and parking lots, and many are killed by cars.
Drive slowly in nēnē crossing zones, especially in national parks.
Named Hawaiʻi's state bird in 1957.

entries.title: Pueo, the Hawaiian owl
entries.summary: The pueo is Hawaiʻi's native short-eared owl, a subspecies found only here. Unlike most owls it hunts by day, hovering over grasslands and fields. It lives on all the main islands and is listed as endangered on Oʻahu.
details: Hawaiian short-eared owl (Asio flammeus sandwichensis), an endemic subspecies.
Active in daylight: watch for it hovering or gliding low over open fields, pastures and grasslands, from sea level to about 8,000 feet.
State-listed as endangered on Oʻahu, where habitat loss is a big threat.
Threats: ground nests eaten by rats, cats and mongoose; vehicle strikes; pesticides in prey.
In Hawaiian tradition, the pueo is an ʻaumakua (family guardian) for some families.
If you find an injured pueo, contact the state DLNR Division of Forestry and Wildlife on your island.

entries.title: Hawaiian honeycreepers (ʻiʻiwi, ʻapapane, ʻakikiki) and the mosquito problem
entries.summary: Hawaiian honeycreepers are colorful native forest birds, like the red ʻiʻiwi and ʻapapane, that evolved from a single finch ancestor into dozens of species. Many are now extinct or endangered, mostly because mosquitoes spread avian malaria. Kauaʻi's ʻakikiki was declared functionally extinct in the wild in 2024.
details: Where to see them: high-elevation native forests such as Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park, Haleakalā (Hosmer Grove) and Kōkeʻe on Kauaʻi. Kula Botanical Garden on Maui reports ʻapapane and ʻamakihi.
Mosquitoes arrived in Hawaiʻi in the 1800s; the birds have no defense against the avian malaria they carry.
Warming lets mosquitoes reach higher, cooler forests that used to be safe for the birds.
ʻAkikiki (Kauaʻi): a few birds left in the wild by 2024; the species is considered functionally extinct in the wild.
Agencies are releasing male mosquitoes carrying Wolbachia, which keeps eggs from hatching, to shrink mosquito numbers.
Help: clean boots and gear between forests, and support native forest groups.

entries.title: Hawaiian monk seal (ʻīlio holo i ka uaua)
entries.summary: One of the most endangered seals in the world, found only in Hawaiʻi. There are about 1,600, most in the remote Northwestern Hawaiian Islands, but more now haul out on main-island beaches. Its Hawaiian name means dog that runs in rough water. Stay at least 50 feet away (150 feet from a mom and pup).
details: About 1,600 range-wide (NOAA, 2024), up from about 1,400 a decade earlier. 34 pups were born in the main Hawaiian Islands in 2024.
Endangered under the Endangered Species Act; harassing one is a crime. It is Hawaiʻi's official state mammal.
Seals sleep on beaches for hours; that's normal. Volunteers often put up a rope or signs around them.
Keep dogs leashed; seals and dogs can pass diseases to each other.
To report a seal on the beach or an injured or entangled one, use NOAA's reporting line: 888-256-9840.
Ask Hawaiʻi's logo is a Hawaiian monk seal.

entries.title: Honu, the Hawaiian green sea turtle
entries.summary: Honu are the sea turtles you'll see snorkeling and resting on beaches. Hawaiʻi is one of only four places in the world where green turtles haul out on land to rest. They're protected by law: stay at least 10 feet away, never touch or feed them, and report injured turtles to 888-256-9840.
details: Protected under the Endangered Species Act (the Hawaiʻi population is listed as threatened).
Basking: turtles come ashore to rest, warm up and avoid tiger sharks. A resting turtle can look dead; look for slow breathing.
Distance: at least 10 feet, on land and in the water.
Most nest in the remote Northwestern Hawaiian Islands, then return to the main islands to feed on seaweed.
Good places to see them from a respectful distance: Laniākea on Oʻahu's North Shore, Hoʻokipa on Maui and Punaluʻu black sand beach on Hawaiʻi Island.
Injured or tangled turtle: NOAA Marine Wildlife Hotline 888-256-9840.

entries.title: Humpback whales and whale season
entries.summary: Thousands of humpback whales come to Hawaiʻi each winter to mate and give birth. They can arrive as early as September and stay into May, with the peak in January and February. The best viewing is between Maui, Lānaʻi and Molokaʻi; stay at least 100 yards away.
details: Season: as early as September through May; peak January and February.
Best areas: the shallow channels between Maui, Lānaʻi and Molokaʻi; Kauaʻi's north coast; the Kohala coast of Hawaiʻi Island. Oʻahu sees fewer, but they're spotted off the south and west shores.
Shore viewing: look for blows and breaches from high lookouts in the morning when the water is calm.
Federal law: stay at least 100 yards away by boat, kayak, board or drone.
They feed in Alaska in summer and fast while in Hawaiʻi.
The waters are protected as the Hawaiian Islands Humpback Whale National Marine Sanctuary.

entries.title: ʻŌpeʻapeʻa, the Hawaiian hoary bat
entries.summary: Hawaiʻi's only native land mammal is a small, endangered bat, the ʻōpeʻapeʻa. Its ancestors flew here from North America. It roosts alone in trees by day and comes out around sunset to hunt insects. It became the official state land mammal in 2015.
details: The only native land mammal in Hawaiʻi; everything else, from pigs to mongoose, was brought by people.
Endangered under federal and state law.
Found on all the main islands except Niʻihau; roosts in trees like ʻōhiʻa, kukui and coconut palms.
Wingspan about one foot; females are a bit larger than males.
Look for it at dusk over open areas, streams and forest edges.
Its ancestors may have first arrived about 1.35 million years ago.

entries.title: Mōlī, the Laysan albatross
entries.summary: Huge seabirds with nearly 7-foot wingspans nest in Hawaiʻi from about November through summer. You can see them at Kaʻena Point on Oʻahu (free, about a 5-mile round-trip hike) and Kīlauea Point National Wildlife Refuge on Kauaʻi. July and August are best for chicks.
details: Arrive and start nesting around November; the season lasts about nine months.
Oʻahu: Kaʻena Point Natural Area Reserve, protected by a predator-proof fence. Free; about 5.4 miles round trip on an exposed, hot trail.
Kauaʻi: Kīlauea Point National Wildlife Refuge on the north shore; small entry fee, check current days and hours.
They can live into their 60s and return to the colony where they hatched.
Most of the world's Laysan albatross nest in the remote Northwestern Hawaiian Islands.
Stay on the trail and well back from nests; don't touch the birds.

entries.title: Humuhumunukunukuāpuaʻa, the state fish
entries.summary: The reef triggerfish with the famous long name is Hawaiʻi's state fish. The name roughly means triggerfish with a pig-like snout. It's common on shallow reefs on every island, so snorkelers spot it at places like Hanauma Bay, Kahaluʻu Beach Park and Poʻipū.
details: Name: humuhumu (triggerfish) + nukunuku (snout) + a (like) + puaʻa (pig). Locals often just say humuhumu.
Named the state fish in 1985 on a temporary basis; made permanent in 2006.
6 to 10 inches long, with tan, yellow and blue bands and a yellow stripe behind the eye.
Territorial: it will chase much bigger fish away from its patch of reef.
Snorkel spots: Hanauma Bay (Oʻahu), Molokini (Maui), Kahaluʻu Beach Park (Hawaiʻi Island), Poʻipū Beach (Kauaʻi).
Don't touch or stand on coral, and use mineral, reef-safe sunscreen.

entries.title: Mongoose, snakes and other animals that don't belong
entries.summary: Many animals you see in Hawaiʻi were brought by people. The mongoose was imported in 1883 to fight rats in sugar fields and now preys on native birds and turtle eggs; it lives on Oʻahu, Maui, Molokaʻi and Hawaiʻi Island but not Kauaʻi or Lānaʻi. Snakes are illegal in Hawaiʻi; report any sighting to 808-643-7378.
details: Mongoose: brought from India in 1883 for rat control; it hunts by day while rats are active at night, so it barely helped. It eats eggs of ground-nesting birds and sea turtles.
Kauaʻi and Lānaʻi have no known mongoose populations; stray ones caught at Kauaʻi's harbor and airport are trapped quickly.
Snakes, large reptiles and many other animals are illegal to own or bring in. Penalties can reach a $200,000 fine and three years in prison.
Amnesty: hand over an illegal animal before an investigation begins and there's no penalty; drop-offs at humane societies, the zoo or state agriculture offices.
Report snakes or illegal animals to the state Pest Hotline: 808-643-PEST (7378).
Other well-known arrivals: feral chickens (common on Kauaʻi), wild pigs, and coquí frogs on Hawaiʻi Island.

entries.title: Shopping tips: tax, kamaʻāina discounts and Hawaiian-made gifts
entries.summary: Prices in Hawaiʻi don't include tax: the general excise tax is added at the register, usually 4.712% on every island. entries.title: Lūʻau on Maui
entries.summary: Maui's best-known lūʻau run about $200 to $360 per adult. In Lāhainā and Kāʻanapali: Old Lāhainā Lūʻau (about $230), Drums of the Pacific at the Hyatt Regency (about $202 to $250) and Myths of Maui at the Royal Lahaina (about $209 to $265). In Wailea: Te Au Moana (about $286 to $325) and The Feast at Mōkapu at Andaz (about $280 to $360).
details: Old Lāhainā Lūʻau: 1251 Front St., Lāhainā; about $230; oceanfront, traditional, tableside meal, unlimited drinks; books up weeks ahead. Phone 808-667-1998.
Drums of the Pacific: Hyatt Regency Maui, Kāʻanapali; about $202 standard, $250 VIP; pan-Polynesian show with fire knife dance.
Myths of Maui: Royal Lahaina Resort, Kāʻanapali Beach; about $209 to $265; running since the 1970s; keiki buffet.
Te Au Moana: Wailea Beach Resort; about $286 to $325; family-style dinner, imu ceremony.
The Feast at Mōkapu: Andaz Maui, Wailea; about $280 to $360; upscale multicourse.
Lāhainā is still rebuilding after the 2023 fire; follow posted road and area closures.

entries.title: Waikīkī boat trips: sunset sails, booze cruises and the Atlantis submarine
entries.summary: Sunset sails leave Waikīkī and Kewalo Basin most evenings around 5 to 5:30 p.m.: BYOB cruises from about $56, catamaran sails about $70 to $123, and dinner-show cruises about $132 to $149. For something different, the Atlantis Submarine dives about 100 feet off Waikīkī (about $168 adults, $75 kids).
details: BYOB sunset cruise: about 90 minutes, from about $56; guests 21+ may bring their own drinks.
Catamaran sails: about 1.5 to 2 hours, about $70 to $123; some include a couple of drinks, others sell drinks on board. Some catamarans board right off Waikīkī Beach.
Dinner and show cruise (Star of Honolulu): 2 to 3 hours, about $132 to $149, with dinner and Hawaiian entertainment.
Most leave Kewalo Basin Harbor or Waikīkī piers; check your confirmation for the exact meeting spot.

Atlantis Submarine: check in at the Hilton Hawaiian Village, ferry out, then about a 40-minute dive to about 100 feet with wrecks and reef. About $168 adults, $75 children; minimum height 36 inches; must climb a ladder.
Winter cruises often spot humpback whales.

entries.title: Surf lessons in Waikīkī
entries.summary: Waikīkī's gentle, rolling waves are the classic place to learn to surf. Beach schools set up right on the sand by the big hotels and offer group, semi-private and private lessons. Everyone must be able to swim, and kids often need private lessons.
details: Where: lessons start on Waikīkī Beach near the Royal Hawaiian, Sheraton Waikiki and Outrigger Waikiki/Duke's, and at the Diamond Head end of the beach.
Formats: group (4 to 5 per instructor), semi-private (2 to 3) and private (1 on 1).
Age rules vary: some schools require private lessons for kids under 12; some group lessons are 13 and up.
All students must be able to swim without help.
Ask what's included: board, leash, rash guard, reef shoes, locker, photos.
On the North Shore, lessons are given in Haleʻiwa when the surf is small (usually summer).

entries.title: Parasailing in Hawaiʻi (seasonal on Maui)
entries.summary: Parasailing runs year-round off Honolulu (from Kewalo Basin and nearby harbors) and in Kona. On Maui it's seasonal: state law bans parasailing off West and South Maui from Dec. 15 to May 15 to protect humpback whales. Most operators let kids 5 and up fly, often tandem.
details: Oʻahu: boats leave Kewalo Basin and nearby slips on Ala Moana Blvd.; arrive 30 minutes early. Typical flights 5 to 8 minutes on 800 to 1,000 feet of line.
Maui: allowed only May 16 to Dec. 14 in West and South Maui waters (Hawaiʻi law, whale protection). Kāʻanapali departures in season.
Hawaiʻi Island: Kona flights run year-round.
Weight rules: solo fliers often need about 160 lb minimum; tandem or triple flights have a combined maximum.
Pregnant guests and people with recent injuries usually can't fly.
Line length isn't the same as height; flights depend on wind and sea conditions.

entries.title: Molokini Crater snorkel trips (Maui)
entries.summary: Molokini is a sunken volcanic crater about three miles off South Maui and a protected Marine Life Conservation District with clear water and lots of reef fish. You can only get there by boat; tours leave from Māʻalaea Harbor or by beach-loading boats in South Maui (Kīhei, Wailea), and often add a second stop at Turtle Town.
details: Departures: Māʻalaea Harbor (handy from West and Central Maui) or South Maui beach-loading boats (handy from Kīhei and Wailea).
Protected area: no fishing or taking marine life, no feeding fish; boats use day-use moorings.
Mornings are usually calmer; trips can be rerouted or canceled for wind and swell.
Many tours include gear, breakfast and lunch; compare total time in the water, not just trip length.
Use mineral, reef-safe sunscreen (required by Maui County).
Don't touch coral or turtles; stay 10 feet from honu.

entries.title: Manta ray night snorkel (Kona, Hawaiʻi Island)
entries.summary: One of Hawaiʻi's most famous experiences: boats leave Keauhou Bay or Honokōhau Harbor near sunset, and you float holding a lit board that draws plankton, and the giant manta rays that come to eat it. Trips take about 2 to 2.5 hours and usually cost about $130 to $180.
details: Sites: Manta Village off Keauhou (south of Kailua-Kona) and Manta Heaven/Garden Eel Cove near the Kona airport.
Boats leave about an hour before sunset; 30 to 45 minutes in the water.
About $130 to $180 per person; wetsuit and gear usually included.
Mantas are wild and don't show every night; some operators offer a free return trip, so check the policy and leave a spare day.
Rules: stay at the surface, don't dive down, chase or touch the mantas; keep fins up near the surface.
Not ideal for people prone to seasickness or nervous in dark open water.

entries.title: Helicopter tours of Kauaʻi
entries.summary: Much of Kauaʻi, including the Nā Pali cliffs, Waimea Canyon's interior, Mount Waiʻaleʻale and Manawaiopuna ("Jurassic") Falls, can only really be seen from the air. Most tours leave Līhuʻe Airport and last about 50 to 65 minutes; doors-off and landing tours are available.
details: Standard tour: about 50 minutes around the island; full-island tours 60 to 65 minutes.
Doors-off: same routes with doors removed; closed-toe shoes, no loose items, stricter weight limits.
Landing tour: about 90 minutes with a stop at a private site.
Most depart Līhuʻe Airport (LIH); some leave from Princeville.
Weather often forces reschedules; book 2 to 4 weeks ahead in peak seasons (December to March, June to August) and leave flexibility.
Safety: check the operator's record and recent reviews; a tour helicopter crashed fatally near Kalalau Beach in March 2026, and the NTSB investigation was ongoing.

entries.title: Oʻahu day trip: the circle island drive
entries.summary: The classic full-day loop: head east past Hālona Blowhole and Makapuʻu, up the windward coast through Waimānalo, Kailua and Kualoa, stop for garlic shrimp in Kahuku, see the big-wave beaches of the North Shore, have shave ice in Haleʻiwa, then come back through the pineapple fields of Central Oʻahu. Plan 8 to 10 hours with stops.
details: 1. Hālona Blowhole Lookout (Hawaiʻi Kai): ocean blowhole and coast views.
2. Makapuʻu Point Lookout: windward views to Rabbit Island. (The upper lookout had weekend closures in fall 2026.)
3. Waimānalo Beach Park: long turquoise beach for a swim.
4. Kailua Beach Park: lunch or coffee in Kailua town.
5. Kualoa Regional Park: views of Mokoliʻi (Chinaman's Hat) and the Kualoa cliffs.
6. Kahuku shrimp trucks: Giovanni's, Romy's or Fumi's for a garlic shrimp plate.
7. Sunset Beach Park: famous winter surf.
8. Haleʻiwa town: Matsumoto Shave Ice (since the 1950s), shops and food trucks.
9. Dole Plantation (Wahiawā): pineapple treats on the drive home.
Driving: about 110 to 130 miles with the loop back; go clockwise early to beat windward traffic. Hanauma Bay and Diamond Head need separate reservations if you add them.

entries.title: Oʻahu half-day trip: southeast coast and the Pali
entries.summary: A half-day loop from Waikīkī around Diamond Head and the rugged southeast shore to Waimānalo and Kailua, then back over the mountains via the Nuʻuanu Pali Lookout. About 40 miles; allow 4 to 5 hours, more if you snorkel at Hanauma Bay.
details: 1. Diamond Head lookouts along Diamond Head Road (the crater hike needs a reservation for non-residents).
2. Hanauma Bay Nature Preserve: reservation required; closed Mondays and Tuesdays.
3. Hālona Blowhole Lookout.
4. Sandy Beach: watch the bodysurfers, but the shorebreak is dangerous.
5. Makapuʻu Point Lookout (or hike the paved Makapuʻu Lighthouse Trail).
6. Waimānalo Beach Park.
7. Kailua: lunch in town, then Kailua Beach.
8. Nuʻuanu Pali Lookout: windy cliffs and the site of a key 1795 battle in Kamehameha's unification of the islands.
Back to Waikīkī down the Pali Highway.

entries.title: Oʻahu day trip: the North Shore
entries.summary: Go up through the middle of the island to Dole Plantation and Haleʻiwa town, then follow the coast past Waimea Bay, Waimea Valley's waterfall, Pipeline and Sunset Beach to the Kahuku shrimp trucks. In winter, watch giant surf; in summer, the same beaches are often calm enough to swim.
details: 1. Dole Plantation (Wahiawā): Dole Whip and the pineapple garden.
2. Haleʻiwa town: shops, food trucks and Matsumoto Shave Ice.
3. Waimea Bay: big-wave surf in winter, swimming and the jumping rock in calm summer seas.
4. Waimea Valley: garden walk to Waimea Falls (admission; Hawaiʻi residents pay less).
5. ʻEhukai Beach Park: home of the Banzai Pipeline.
6. Sunset Beach.
7. Kahuku: garlic shrimp at Giovanni's, Romy's or Fumi's, or Mike's Huli-Huli Chicken.
Return via H-2 (faster) or continue down the windward coast for the full circle.
Winter surf is deadly: watch from the sand when lifeguards post warnings. Parking along Kamehameha Highway fills early.

entries.title: Oʻahu day trip: Pearl Harbor and historic Honolulu
entries.summary: A history-filled day: the USS Arizona Memorial at Pearl Harbor in the morning, then downtown Honolulu for ʻIolani Palace, the King Kamehameha statue and Kawaiahaʻo Church, lunch in Chinatown, and Foster Botanical Garden or the Bishop Museum in the afternoon.
details: 1. Pearl Harbor National Memorial: free, but reserve USS Arizona program tickets on Recreation.gov; no bags allowed; parking $7.
2. ʻIolani Palace: tours must be booked ahead; no walk-ups.
3. King Kamehameha Statue, across from the palace at Aliʻiōlani Hale.
4. Kawaiahaʻo Church, Honolulu's historic coral-block church.
5. Chinatown: lunch, lei stands and markets.
6. Foster Botanical Garden (open 9 to 4; $5 adults, $3 Hawaiʻi residents).
7. Optional: Bishop Museum (daily 9 to 5) for Hawaiian history and culture.
Tip: start early at Pearl Harbor, where morning tickets go first.

entries.title: Maui day trip: the Road to Hāna
entries.summary: The famous winding drive along Maui's rainforest coast: start early from Paʻia, stop at the Garden of Eden Arboretum, the Keʻanae Peninsula for Aunty Sandy's banana bread, Halfway to Hāna at mile 17, and Waiʻānapanapa's black-sand beach (reservation required), then Hāna town. About 52 miles from Kahului with hundreds of curves and one-lane bridges; plan a full day and return the way you came.
details: 1. Paʻia: last easy stop for gas, food and restrooms.
2. Garden of Eden Arboretum (half mile past mile marker 10): daily 8 to 4; $20 adults.
3. Keʻanae Peninsula: lava-rock coast and Aunty Sandy's banana bread.
4. Halfway to Hāna stand (mile marker 17): banana bread since 1982.
5. Waiʻānapanapa State Park: non-residents must reserve a time slot in advance or will be turned away.
6. Hāna town: a quiet, small town; please respect private property and residents.
Leave by 7 a.m., fill up the tank in Paʻia, and don't stop in the road or block bridges; pull fully off to let locals pass.
Return the same way; check your rental agreement before driving the rough back road past Kīpahulu.

entries.title: Maui day trip: Haleakalā and Upcountry
entries.summary: Drive up Haleakalā (sunrise needs a reservation; daytime visits just need the park entry pass), then come down through cool Upcountry Maui: Kula Botanical Garden, the paniolo (cowboy) town of Makawao with Komoda Store's famous cream puffs, then Paʻia and the Hoʻokipa lookout to watch windsurfers and turtles.
details: 1. Haleakalā National Park summit: sunrise entry (3 to 7 a.m.) needs a Recreation.gov reservation; any time needs the park pass. It's often below freezing before dawn.
2. Kula Botanical Garden (Kekaulike Road, about 3,300 ft): protea, orchids and native plants.
3. Makawao: paniolo town with galleries and T. Komoda Store and Bakery, open since 1916, known for cream puffs and stick donuts. Go early; it sells out.
4. Paʻia: lunch and shops.
5. Hoʻokipa Beach Park lookout: windsurfers and resting honu (keep 10 feet away).
The summit road climbs from sea level to 10,000 feet in about 2 hours; bring layers and fill up on gas.

entries.title: Maui day trip: ʻĪao Valley and the West Maui coast
entries.summary: Start at ʻĪao Valley (reservation required for non-residents), then drive the coast to West Maui: Kāʻanapali's beach and Whalers Village, Nāpili and Kapalua, and the Honolua Bay lookout. Lāhainā is still rebuilding after the August 2023 fire; drive through respectfully and follow posted closures.
details: 1. ʻĪao Valley State Monument (Wailuku): 7 a.m. to 6 p.m.; non-residents reserve ahead ($5 entry, $10 parking).
2. Pali coast drive on Honoapiʻilani Highway: whale watching in winter from pullouts.
3. Lāhainā: still rebuilding; many areas remain closed. Please don't sightsee in burned areas.
4. Kāʻanapali Beach and Whalers Village: shopping, lunch, returning Lāhainā businesses.
5. Nāpili Bay and Kapalua Bay: calm-water swimming in summer.
6. Honolua Bay lookout: famous winter surf; snorkel in calm summer conditions.
Beyond Honolua the road (Kahekili Highway) becomes narrow and rough; many visitors turn back here.

entries.title: Kauaʻi day trip: the North Shore drive
entries.summary: From Līhuʻe, drive up the east side through Kapaʻa to the Kīlauea Lighthouse, the Hanalei Valley Lookout over the taro fields, Hanalei town and Hāʻena State Park at the end of the road (reservation required for visitors).

2. Kīlauea Point National Wildlife Refuge and lighthouse: Wednesday to Saturday, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.; reserve on Recreation.gov ($11 adults); great for seabirds and albatross in season.
3. Hanalei Valley Lookout: taro fields under green mountains.
4. Hanalei town: lunch, JoJo's Shave Ice, Hanalei Bay.
5. Hāʻena State Park and Kēʻē Beach: reservation required at gohaena.com; open 7 a.m. to 6:45 p.m.; the Kalalau Trail is open to Hanakāpīʻai only (Oct. 2026).
Past Hanalei the road crosses several one-lane bridges: yield in groups of five to seven cars.

entries.title: Kauaʻi day trip: Waimea Canyon and the West Side
entries.summary: Head west from Poʻipū or Līhuʻe through Hanapēpē's art town and historic Waimea town, then climb to the Waimea Canyon Lookout, the "Grand Canyon of the Pacific." entries.title: Hawaiʻi Island day trip: Hilo and the volcano
entries.summary: Start in Hilo with the free Liliʻuokalani Gardens and a loco moco at Café 100 or Ken's House of Pancakes (Hilo is where the loco moco was born), see Rainbow Falls, then drive about 45 minutes up to Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park to see Kīlauea and, if it's erupting, the glow in Halemaʻumaʻu crater.
details: 1. Liliʻuokalani Gardens (Banyan Drive): free Japanese garden on Hilo Bay, open 24 hours.
2. Loco moco: Café 100 (969 Kīlauea Ave., serving it since 1949) or Ken's House of Pancakes (1730 Kamehameha Ave., open 24 hours).
3. Rainbow Falls (Wailuku River State Park): short walk; rainbows on sunny mornings.
4. Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park: $30 per car for 7 days, card only. Kīlauea Visitor Center first for eruption updates.
5. Kīlauea overlooks: eruption activity changes constantly; check the USGS Hawaiian Volcano Observatory. Lots can fill by 10 a.m.
6. Volcano Village: dinner and a cozy night if you want to see the glow after dark.
Volcanic gas can affect people with heart or breathing problems, pregnant people and young children.
Add-on north of Hilo: ʻAkaka Falls and the Hawaiʻi Tropical Botanical Garden.

entries.title: Hawaiian food explained: laulau, kālua pig, poi and more
entries.summary: A traditional Hawaiian plate usually has laulau or kālua pig with poi, lomi salmon, chicken long rice or squid lūʻau, and haupia for dessert. Poi, pounded taro, is the heart of the meal; eat it alongside the salty dishes.
details: Laulau: pork (often with butterfish) wrapped in taro leaves and steamed for hours.
Kālua pig: smoky, salty pulled pork, traditionally cooked in an imu (underground oven).
Poi: cooked taro pounded with water; sour poi is older, fresh poi is sweeter.
Squid lūʻau: squid or octopus with young taro leaves in coconut milk.
Lomi salmon: diced salted salmon with tomato and onion, served cold.
Pipikaula: salted, dried beef, broiled until crisp, like Hawaiian jerky.
Chicken long rice: glass noodles in ginger-chicken broth.
Haupia: firm coconut pudding squares. Kūlolo: dense baked taro and coconut.
Poke: raw cubed fish (often ʻahi) seasoned with salt, shoyu, sesame oil and onion.
Ask for a Hawaiian plate to try several at once.
Hours change and many small spots sell out or close early; call or check online before you go.

entries.title: Highway Inn (Waipahu and Kakaʻako)
entries.summary: One of Oʻahu's best-known Hawaiian food restaurants, started in 1947 by Seiichi and Nancy Toguchi in Waipahu. Locations in Waipahu and Kakaʻako; try the Tasting Plate (kālua pig, chicken long rice, lomi salmon, squid lūʻau). Closes at 3 p.m. on Sundays.

Kakaʻako location opened in 2013, near Ala Moana; adds fish tacos, kālua pig nachos and laulau spring rolls.
Its Bishop Museum café was rebranded Tūtū's Place in 2025.

entries.title: Getting to and around Molokaʻi
entries.summary: You can only fly to Molokaʻi: the passenger ferry from Lāhainā stopped in 2016 (Maui County plans a new one around 2029). Mokulele Airlines flies small planes from Honolulu and Kahului to Hoʻolehua Airport (MKK), and Lānaʻi Air flies from Honolulu. Alamo is the only rental car company and there's no rideshare, so book a car with your flight.
details: Flights: Mokulele Airlines (Honolulu and Kahului to MKK); Lānaʻi Air from Honolulu (uses a hangar on Kaulele Place; courtesy shuttle needs 48 hours' notice).
No ferry since October 2016. Maui County plans to build boats from 2027 and start Molokaʻi service in 2029.
Rental cars: Alamo only at the airport, with a small fleet. Book early. No Uber or Lyft.
A free Maui Economic Opportunity bus runs weekdays with limited Saturday service; call 808-553-3218 to confirm times.
Gas is pricier and there are only a couple of stations; fill up in Kaunakakai.
Kaunakakai is the only town: groceries, bank, post office, restaurants. Stores close early and Sundays are quiet.

entries.title: Kalaupapa: the lookout and the paused tours
entries.summary: Kalaupapa is the remote peninsula below Molokaʻi's sea cliffs where thousands of people with Hansen's disease (leprosy) were forcibly isolated from 1866 to 1969. You can see it from the Kalaupapa Lookout in Pālāʻau State Park (free, 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.). Public tours to the settlement were paused after a single National Park Service tour on July 9, 2026, with no restart date.
details: Kalaupapa Lookout, Pālāʻau State Park: free; open daily 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.; the settlement is about 1,600 feet below.
Public tours: the National Park Service ran one guided hiking tour on July 9, 2026, then paused tours after community protests; no timeline to resume.
The Pali Trail down the cliff crosses private land and isn't open to general visitors.
History: from 1866 to 1969, people with Hansen's disease were sent here; Saint Damien and Saint Marianne Cope served the community.
Kalaupapa National Historical Park remains home to a small number of former patients; please respect their privacy.

entries.title: Hālawa Valley guided hike to Moʻoula Falls (Molokaʻi)
entries.summary: Hālawa Valley at Molokaʻi's east end is one of the oldest settled valleys in Hawaiʻi. The hike to 250-foot Moʻoula (Moaʻula) Falls crosses private land, so you must go with a guide: the Solatorio ʻohana leads tours at 9 a.m. Monday, Tuesday and Thursday through Saturday, about 3.4 miles round trip with two river crossings, $100 adults and $65 kids 4 to 12.
details: Guided only: the valley is privately owned.
Solatorio ʻohana tours: 9 a.m. Mon., Tue., Thu., Fri., Sat. (closed Wed. and Sun.). About 3.4 miles round trip with two stream crossings.
Price: $100 adults, $65 kids 4 to 12; two-person minimum.
Another guide, Mystical Molokai, has also led valley hikes.
Wear closed-toe shoes that can get wet; expect mud and mosquitoes.
Local lore: float a ti leaf on the pool; if it sinks, don't swim.

entries.title: Molokaʻi day trip: the East End to Hālawa
entries.summary: Drive east from Kaunakakai along Kamehameha V Highway, the slow coastal road past old Hawaiian fishponds and St. Joseph Church, built by Father Damien in 1876, to the end of the road at Hālawa Valley and Hālawa Beach Park. Pick up hot bread or lunch in Kaunakakai first; there are few services out east.
details: 1. Kaunakakai: gas up, then Kanemitsu Bakery for breakfast or bread.
2. St. Joseph Church (Kamalō): small wooden church built by Father Damien in 1876.
3. The coast road: ancient fishponds along the shore; the road gets narrow and winding past mile 20. Drive slowly and wave.
4. Hālawa Valley and Hālawa Beach Park at the end of the road; book the guided falls hike ahead.
Plan most of a day; same road back.

entries.title: Visiting Molokaʻi respectfully: the Friendly Isle
entries.summary: Molokaʻi is rural and proud of it, with a long history of resisting big resort development. Wave to other drivers, pull over to let locals pass, ask before parking or walking on land that may be private, buy from local farm stands and markets, and plan around early-closing stores and quiet Sundays.
details: Wave at oncoming drivers; pull over if cars stack up behind you.
Much land is private: ask before parking or walking; stay on public beaches and parks.
Stores close early and Sundays are quiet; shop on a weekday afternoon.
Support local businesses: farm stands, Kanemitsu Bakery, small markets.
Drones: check rules and get permission before flying.
Many places have limited or no cell service; download maps before you go.

entries.title: Getting to and around Lānaʻi
entries.summary: Most visitors arrive on the Expeditions ferry from Māʻalaea Harbor on Maui: three round trips a day, about 1 hour 10 minutes each way (Māʻalaea departs 6:30 a.m., 11 a.m., 3:30 p.m.; Mānele departs 8:30 a.m., 1 p.m., 5:30 p.m.). details: Ferry: Expeditions, Māʻalaea Harbor (Maui) to Mānele Harbor (Lānaʻi). Reservations 800-695-2624. Times can change; check the booking calendar.
Maui County plans to take over the route with a contracted operator around mid-2027.
Fly: small-plane service into Lānaʻi Airport (LNY).

Getting around: Lānaʻi City has one main paved road network; beyond it, roads are dirt and cinder. Dollar Rent A Car Lānaʻi rents Jeep Wranglers for off-road routes; Four Seasons guests can rent Jeeps.
Rental contracts often exclude damage on unpaved roads; read yours.
Hulopoʻe Beach is a short walk or ride from the ferry dock, so a day trip without a car is possible.

entries.title: Hulopoʻe Bay and Puʻu Pehe (Sweetheart Rock), Lānaʻi
entries.summary: Lānaʻi's best beach, Hulopoʻe Bay, is a protected marine area with clear water and reef for snorkeling, right near the Mānele ferry dock. A short trail from the beach leads to the cliffs overlooking Puʻu Pehe, the sea stack called Sweetheart Rock. Spinner dolphins often visit the bay in the morning.
details: Hulopoʻe Beach Park: white sand, calm on most days, good snorkeling on the reef; restrooms and showers.
It's a protected marine area: don't take shells, rocks or marine life, and don't feed fish.
Puʻu Pehe (Sweetheart Rock): a short, rocky trail from the left end of Hulopoʻe to the cliff overlook. Stay back from the edge.
Spinner dolphins may come in to rest; federal rules say stay at least 50 yards away and don't swim with them.
Walkable from the Mānele ferry harbor, so it works on a ferry day trip.

entries.title: Keahiakawelo (Garden of the Gods) and Polihua, Lānaʻi
entries.summary: Keahiakawelo is a field of red, orange and purple rock formations about 4 miles from Lānaʻi City on Polihua Road. The first 1.3 miles are paved, then gravel; a regular SUV can reach Keahiakawelo, but continuing to remote Polihua Beach needs a real 4WD. Don't stack or take rocks; it's a culturally important place.
details: Distance: about 4.2 miles from Lānaʻi City; about 10.8 miles (45 minutes) to Polihua Beach.
Road: paved for 1.3 miles, then gravel and dirt; past Keahiakawelo it's loose cinder and steep, 4WD only.
Please don't stack rocks or build cairns, and take nothing home. In Hawaiian tradition the place is tied to a contest between two kahuna.
Polihua Beach: swimming is not safe (steep shore break, strong current, no lifeguard, no phone service).
Swim and snorkel at Hulopoʻe Bay instead.
Also on the north shore: Shipwreck Beach (Kaiolohia), with an old wreck offshore, reached by 4WD.

entries.title: Lānaʻi day trip from Maui
entries.summary: Take the morning Expeditions ferry from Māʻalaea, snorkel Hulopoʻe Bay and see Sweetheart Rock, head up to Lānaʻi City for lunch (Blue Ginger Café is a favorite) and the Lānaʻi Culture & Heritage Center on Dole Park, then, with a Jeep, drive out to Keahiakawelo (Garden of the Gods) before catching the last ferry back.

entries.title: Hāpuna Beach State Recreation Area
entries.summary: One of Hawaiʻi Island's widest white-sand beaches, on the Kohala Coast about 30 minutes north of the Kona airport. It has lifeguards, but rip currents and shorebreak get dangerous when surf is up. Non-residents pay an entry fee plus parking; Hawaiʻi residents get in free.
details: Hours: 7 a.m. to 7:30 p.m.; the gates close at 8 p.m.
Fees for non-residents: $5 per person (credit card only) plus $10 per vehicle for parking. Hawaiʻi residents with ID are free.
Lifeguards are on duty. In winter and whenever surf is high, watch for strong shorebreak and rip currents; ask the lifeguard before you swim.
Facilities include restrooms, showers and picnic pavilions. The A-frame cabins are closed.
The Ala Kahakai coastal trail links Hāpuna to Kaunaʻoa (Mauna Kea Beach) to the north.
Shade is limited, so bring an umbrella and reef-safe sunscreen.

entries.title: Papakōlea Green Sand Beach hike
entries.summary: A rare olivine green-sand beach near Ka Lae (South Point). The walk is about 4.5 miles round trip from the end of South Point Road, 3 to 4 hours with no shade or water and strong wind. Informal $20 cash truck rides operate without commercial permits, according to DHHL, and rental-car contracts ban driving the jeep road.
details: Length: about 4.5 miles round trip over a rutted dirt road; allow 3 to 4 hours.
No shade, no water, no restrooms at the beach, and the wind is often strong. Bring plenty of water, a hat and sturdy shoes.
The land belongs to the Department of Hawaiian Home Lands (DHHL), and residents live there; be respectful.
Truck rides: drivers ask about $20 cash per person, but DHHL says they hold no commercial permits. Rental-car contracts prohibit driving your own car down the jeep road.
No lifeguards. The cove gets strong surf and currents, so many people just look and don't swim. The final climb down to the sand is steep.
Cell service is spotty. Don't take any sand; it's part of the place.

entries.title: Punaluʻu Black Sand Beach
entries.summary: Hawaiʻi Island's best-known black-sand beach, in Kaʻū between Volcano and South Point. Green sea turtles often rest on the sand: stay at least 10 feet away. Lifeguards are on duty during the day, and you shouldn't take any black sand home.
details: Getting there: off Highway 11 in Kaʻū; turn makai (toward the ocean) on Alanui Road between mile markers 56 and 57. It's about 45 minutes from Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park.
Lifeguards are posted from about 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m.
Honu (green sea turtles) bask here; keep at least 10 feet away and don't touch or feed them.
The small cove is the calmest swimming spot. Lava rock and cold freshwater springs are common, so wear water shoes.
Taking black sand is prohibited and harms the beach.
Restrooms, showers and picnic pavilions are available; the lot is free.

entries.title: Pololū Valley Trail
entries.summary: A short but steep trail at the end of Highway 270 in North Kohala, dropping about 400 feet to a boulder-and-black-sand beach. It was closed for maintenance in May 2026, led by the community group Protect Pololū ʻOhana, and a management plan with reservations is in the works. Check the current status before you go.
details: Length: about 0.6 mile each way and roughly 400 feet of elevation; it's slick and rocky, so wear real shoes.
May 2026: the trail closed temporarily for maintenance led by Protect Pololū ʻOhana with DLNR. A management plan and a future reservation system have been announced.
The lookout at the end of the road is the easy option and has the classic valley view.
Don't swim at the beach: there are no lifeguards, and strong currents and big surf are common.
Parking at the end of the road is very limited; don't block the road or residents' driveways.

details: The Waipiʻo Valley Lookout at the end of Highway 240 in Kukuihaele is open and free.

entries.title: Mauna Kea summit and Visitor Information Station
entries.summary: Mauna Kea's free Visitor Information Station sits at 9,200 feet, open about 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. You need 4WD to drive past it, the summit closes from 30 minutes after sunset to 30 minutes before sunrise, and children under 16 aren't allowed beyond the station. It's a sacred place, named a Traditional Cultural Property in March 2025.
details: Visitor Information Station (VIS): 9,200 feet on the Mauna Kea Access Road off Saddle Road (Route 200); free; about 9 a.m. to 9 p.m.
Above the VIS, a 4WD vehicle is required (low gear, about 4,600 feet of climb). Most rental contracts forbid the summit road, so a tour is often the practical choice.
The summit is closed from 30 minutes after sunset to 30 minutes before sunrise. Watch the sunset, then go down.

Altitude: no one under 16 past the VIS, and don't go up within 24 hours of scuba diving. People who are pregnant or have heart or lung problems should not go up. Spend about 30 minutes at the VIS first to adjust.
The public stargazing telescope program stopped in 2019. Commercial summit and stargazing tours run about $230 to $290 or more.
It's very cold at the summit (often near freezing), so bring warm layers. Mauna Kea is sacred to Native Hawaiians: stay on roads and trails and don't stack rocks.

entries.title: Kahaluʻu Beach Park (Kona snorkeling)
entries.summary: Kona's easiest beginner snorkel spot, on Aliʻi Drive about 5 miles south of Kailua-Kona. A shallow reef keeps the bay calm most days and honu are common. Lifeguards are on duty 9:30 a.m. to 4:45 p.m., and non-residents pay $12 for four hours of parking.
details: Parking: non-residents pay $12 for four hours, 7 a.m. to 7 p.m., through ParkMobile zone 13300 or at the info tent. Hawaiʻi residents and visitors with disabilities can register for a free pass. The lot fills at midday and on weekends.
Lifeguards: daily 9:30 a.m. to 4:45 p.m.
Entry is over slippery lava rock; water shoes help. Enter at the channel in front of the lifeguard tower, and stay inside the second tower, where the surf zone starts.
A current pulls north and out to sea; it's usually mild but gets stronger with big swell. Look up now and then to check your position.
Volunteers from the Kahaluʻu Bay Education Center (ReefTeach) are on the sand daily to help; free mineral sunscreen dispensers are at the pavilion from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m.
Don't stand on the coral, and give turtles plenty of space. Restrooms, showers and a pavilion are available.

entries.title: Two Step (Hōnaunau Bay) snorkeling
entries.summary: One of Hawaiʻi Island's best snorkel spots: a lava-shelf entry at the Hōnaunau Bay boat ramp, next to Puʻuhonua o Hōnaunau National Historical Park, about 40 minutes south of Kailua-Kona. You may not snorkel from the park's Keoneʻele Cove, and parking is tight, so arrive early.
details: Entry: the natural lava 'two steps' at the Hōnaunau Bay boat ramp, which Hawaiʻi County manages. It's just outside the national park.
Snorkelers may not enter the water at Keoneʻele Cove inside Puʻuhonua o Hōnaunau.
Parking: the park lot is small and fills by midday. The park asks snorkelers to park outside the gate on the one-way public road. Paid private lots nearby are also common.
Don't use the park's restrooms to change or rinse off.
Safety: check surf first, snorkel with a buddy, and watch for boats, since it's a working boat ramp. There are no lifeguards. Don't touch or stand on coral.
Combine it with a walk through Puʻuhonua o Hōnaunau, the restored place of refuge (park entrance fee applies).

entries.title: Kīlauea Iki Trail (Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park)
entries.summary: The park's signature day hike: a roughly 3.3-mile loop (allow 2 to 3 hours) that drops about 400 feet through rainforest and crosses the floor of the 1959 Kīlauea Iki lava lake, which still steams. The trail and overlook are open.
details: Length: about 3.3 miles as a loop from the Kīlauea Iki Overlook, with about 400 feet of descent and climb. Allow 2 to 3 hours.
Status: the overlook and trail are open (NPS, March 2026). Some Kīlauea summit areas near Uēkahuna remain closed after recent eruptive episodes, so check the park's alerts page before you go.
Stay on the ahu (rock cairns) across the crater floor, and don't go into cracks or steaming vents.
The crater floor is exposed and can be hot or wet within the same hour. Bring water, rain gear and sun protection.
Park entrance fee required. Nāhuku (Thurston Lava Tube) is nearby; bring a flashlight, since its lights are out.
If you smell sulfur or the air is hazy, people with heart or breathing problems should limit exposure.

details: Free entry and a free paved lot; open about 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. (county posted hours).

Snorkeling: beginner-friendly inside the breakwater. Stay in the marked zone, since the current picks up near the open end.
The water is cooler and visibility more moderate than on the Kona side, because of freshwater flowing in.
Honu often rest here; stay at least 10 feet away on land or in the water.

entries.title: Pīpīwai Trail, Hāna (bamboo forest and Waimoku Falls)
entries.summary: Maui's most famous hike, in the Kīpahulu District of Haleakalā National Park past Hāna. It's 4 miles round trip with about 800 feet of gain, passing a giant banyan and a bamboo boardwalk on the way to the roughly 400-foot Waimoku Falls. The national park entrance fee is $30 per car, card only.
details: Length: 4 miles round trip, about 800 feet of gain; allow 2 to 3 hours.
Fee: $30 per private vehicle (good for 3 days at both Haleakalā districts), $15 per person on foot or bike. Cards only.
Highlights: Makahiku Falls overlook, a giant banyan (stay off its roots), a bamboo forest on a boardwalk, and the roughly 400-foot Waimoku Falls at the end.
Flash floods and falling rocks happen without warning. Stay behind the signs, stay off the stream, and don't walk under the falls.
As of early October 2026 the trail is open, the Pools of ʻOheʻo are closed to swimming (you can view them from Kūloa Point), and the main restrooms are closed for repairs.
It's about 2.5 to 3 hours' drive from Kahului on the Road to Hāna, so start early and treat it as a daylight hike.
