entries.title: Sliding Sands (Keoneheʻeheʻe) Trail, Haleakalā
entries.summary: The trail into Haleakalā crater, starting at the summit visitor center parking lot at about 10,000 feet. It drops almost 2,500 feet across cinder slopes to the crater floor. Going down is easy; climbing back up at altitude takes about twice as long.
details: Trailhead: Haleakalā Visitor Center parking lot (summit district). Restrooms and water are only at the visitor center.

Options: a short walk to the first overlook (0.5 mile round trip); 3.9 miles one way to the crater floor; about 5.6 miles to Kapalaoa Cabin; or about 11 miles through to the Halemauʻu trailhead (arrange a car shuttle).
Almost 2,500 feet of descent, all of which you climb back out. The park advises allowing twice as long to come up as to go down.
It's often cold, windy and very sunny at 10,000 feet. Bring layers, plenty of water, sun protection and food.
Park entrance fee required. A separate sunrise reservation is needed only to enter the summit district between 3 and 7 a.m.
Stay on the trail; the crater's plants (including the ʻāhinahina, silversword) are fragile and protected.

details: Length: about 5 miles round trip, about 1,500 feet of gain; allow 3 to 4 hours. Rated moderate.

Getting there: from Kahului, take Highway 340 (Kahekili Highway) north past Waiheʻe, then turn up the road at Maluhia Boy Scout Camp to the small trailhead lot.

entries.title: Hoapili Trail (King's Highway), La Perouse Bay
entries.summary: An ancient Hawaiian coastal path, rebuilt in 1824, across the jagged lava fields of South Maui's last lava flow. Most people go out and back from La Perouse Bay to Kanaio Beach: about 5.5 miles and 4 hours with no shade. Start early and bring lots of water.
details: Start: the La Perouse Bay parking area, where Mākena Road dead-ends about 3 miles past Big Beach (Mākena).
Length: about 5.5 miles round trip to Kanaio Beach, about 4 hours. Even an hour gives a good feel for it.
Terrain: sharp ʻaʻā lava. Wear sturdy shoes, not slippers.
No shade, water or reliable cell service. Go early in the morning to beat the heat.
The surf spot 'Laps' early on gets dangerous during big south swells. The trail passes historic sites; look, don't touch or move stones.
Nearby: the ʻĀhihi-Kīnaʻu reserve and La Perouse Bay, where spinner dolphins often rest; keep your distance.

Parking: D.T. Fleming Beach Park has the largest lot. The small lots at Kapalua Bay and the Dragon's Teeth trailhead fill early.

entries.title: Hanakāpīʻai Falls hike (Nāpali Coast)

details: Reservations: non-residents need an entry reservation (and parking or a shuttle seat) from gohaena.com, up to 30 days ahead. Hawaiʻi residents with ID enter free.

Don't swim at Hanakāpīʻai Beach. Strong rip currents have drowned many people.
The trail is rocky and muddy; wear real hiking shoes and bring plenty of water.

entries.title: Moving to Hawaiʻi: first 30 days checklist
entries.summary: The key tasks for new residents in roughly the order they come up: transfer your driver's license within 30 days of becoming a resident, register or permit your car within 30 days of its arrival, sign up for emergency alerts, set up utilities, enroll keiki in school and register to vote. Each county runs its own DMV, so book appointments early.
details: Driver's license: transfer within 30 days of establishing residency (renting a home, taking a job here, enrolling kids or registering to vote all count). You'll take the written test, not a road test. See the driver's license entry.
Car: within 30 days of the car's arrival, register it in Hawaiʻi or get an out-of-state permit; either needs a Hawaiʻi safety check first.
Pets: start the rabies paperwork at least 4 months before you fly, or your pet may face up to 120 days of quarantine.
Emergency: sign up for your county's alerts (for example HNL.INFO on Oʻahu) and build a 14-day supply kit.
Utilities: electricity is the big bill here; ask about solar, ceiling fans and time-of-use rates.
School: enroll at the home school for your address; kids need a Hawaiʻi TB clearance and a recent physical.
Kamaʻāina rates: many attractions, parks and shops give resident discounts once you have a Hawaiʻi ID.
Register to vote: Hawaiʻi votes entirely by mail; register online with the Office of Elections once you have a Hawaiʻi ID.

entries.title: Transferring your driver's license to Hawaiʻi
entries.summary: New residents must switch to a Hawaiʻi license within 30 days of establishing residency. With a valid U.S. license you skip the road test but must pass the written knowledge test, apply in person at your county DMV, and bring original documents. An 8-year license for ages 25 to 71 is $40.
details: Deadline: 30 days after you become a resident (renting or buying a home, taking a Hawaiʻi job, enrolling kids in school, registering to vote or registering a car).
Test: written knowledge test only for valid U.S. license holders ($2 online). Study the Hawaiʻi Driver's Manual.

Bring originals or certified copies (no notarized copies): proof of name and birth date, legal U.S. presence, Social Security number (recommended) and two proofs of Hawaiʻi address. If your name changed, bring the marriage certificate or court order.
Fees: $40 for an 8-year license (ages 25 to 71). Card payments carry a small convenience fee.
Each county runs its own DMV (Honolulu, Maui, Hawaiʻi and Kauaʻi). Book an appointment; on Oʻahu use alohaq.org.
You get a 60-day paper temporary; the card arrives by mail in about 6 to 8 weeks. Hawaiʻi cards are REAL ID compliant (gold star) by default.
Non-drivers can get a Hawaiʻi State ID with similar documents.

entries.title: Registering a car you bring to Hawaiʻi
entries.summary: You have 30 days after your car arrives to either register it in Hawaiʻi or get an out-of-state permit, which keeps your mainland plates valid until they expire. Either way, the car must pass a Hawaiʻi safety inspection first. On Oʻahu the permit is $5 at a satellite city hall, by appointment.
details: Timeline: 30 days from the vehicle's arrival.
Step 1: get a Hawaiʻi safety inspection at a certified station (many gas stations and repair shops). Bring your registration and proof of insurance.
Step 2 (option A): get an out-of-state permit ($5 on Oʻahu) that lets you keep your mainland plates until their registration expires.

Step 2 (option B): register the car in Hawaiʻi and get local plates. Bring the shipping bill of lading, title or lienholder info, out-of-state registration, safety check and Hawaiʻi insurance. Registration fees are based partly on vehicle weight.
On Oʻahu, book at alohaq.org; neighbor islands use their county DMV offices.
Safety checks are required every year for most cars (new cars get a longer first period).

entries.title: Bringing a dog or cat to Hawaiʻi (avoiding quarantine)
entries.summary: Hawaiʻi is rabies-free, so dogs and cats must meet strict rules or face up to 120 days of quarantine. To qualify for same-day Direct Airport Release in Honolulu, start at least four months ahead: microchip, two rabies shots, a FAVN blood test, then a 120-day wait from the blood draw. Paperwork is due 10 days before arrival with a $185 fee.
details: Order matters: microchip first (ISO 11784/11785), then two rabies vaccines at least 30 days apart, then the FAVN blood test (result 0.5 IU/mL or higher).
Wait: 120 days counted from the date the blood was drawn. It can't be shortened.
Within 14 days of arrival: a USDA-accredited vet's health certificate and a tick treatment.
Send documents to the Animal Quarantine Station at least 10 business days before arrival. Direct Airport Release fee: $185 per pet.
Miss a step and your pet goes to the Animal Quarantine Station in Hālawa Valley, Oʻahu, for up to 120 days (about $30 a day).
Budget roughly $835 to $1,370 per pet for tests, vet visits, fees and airline charges.
Banned pets include snakes, ferrets, gerbils and hamsters; most reptiles need permits.

entries.title: Renting in Hawaiʻi: tenant rights basics
entries.summary: Hawaiʻi's landlord-tenant code caps the security deposit at one month's rent (plus up to one more month as a pet deposit). The landlord must return it within 14 days after you move out, give 2 days' notice before entering, and give 45 days' notice to raise rent or end a month-to-month rental.
details: Security deposit: up to one month's rent; a separate pet deposit of up to one month is allowed.
Return: within 14 days after the tenancy ends, with a written list of any deductions and repair costs.
Entry: at least 2 days' notice for non-emergencies, at reasonable hours.
Month-to-month: the landlord needs 45 days' written notice to end it or to raise rent. Rent can't go up during a fixed lease unless the lease allows it.
Late fees are capped at 8% of the rent due and must be in the lease.
Scams are common: never wire money or pay a deposit before seeing the place and confirming the owner.
Questions: the state Office of Consumer Protection runs a landlord-tenant information line.

entries.title: Utility bills in Hawaiʻi: electric, water, internet
entries.summary: Electricity is Hawaiʻi's biggest surprise for newcomers: about 40 cents per kWh on Kauaʻi, 42 on Oʻahu, 46 on Hawaiʻi Island and 47 on Maui, and higher on Molokaʻi and Lānaʻi. A 3-bedroom house with air conditioning can run $400 to $580 a month for power alone.
details: Electric rates (late 2026, all-in averages): Kauaʻi about 40¢/kWh, Oʻahu about 42¢, Hawaiʻi Island about 46¢, Maui about 47¢, Molokaʻi about 56¢, Lānaʻi about 58¢. They change monthly with fuel costs.
Typical electric bills: a 1-bedroom condo without AC about $110 to $160; a 3-bedroom house with AC about $400 to $580.
Water and sewer for a house: Honolulu about $165 to $220 a month (sewer is often the bigger part); other counties lower. Condos usually include these in association fees.
Internet: Spectrum about $50 to $90, Hawaiian Telcom fiber about $55 to $90 where available, 5G home internet about $50 to $70, Starlink about $80 to $120 plus equipment.
Propane runs about $5.50 to $7.50 a gallon. Solar panels and fans cut bills sharply.

entries.title: Health insurance through work (Prepaid Health Care Act)
entries.summary: Hawaiʻi is the only state that requires most employers to provide health insurance. Once you work at least 20 hours a week for four weeks in a row (and earn at least a set minimum monthly wage), your employer must offer coverage, and your share of the premium can't exceed 1.5% of your wages.
details: Eligibility: 20 or more hours a week, after 4 consecutive weeks, with monthly wages of at least 86.67 times the state minimum hourly wage.
Your cost: no more than 1.5% of your monthly wages for your own coverage; the employer pays at least half the premium and covers the rest.
It covers the employee; family coverage is often offered but isn't required by this law.
Run by the state Disability Compensation Division (Department of Labor and Industrial Relations), under Chapter 393, HRS.
Self-employed or between jobs: look at HealthCare.gov marketplace plans or Med-QUEST (Medicaid).

entries.title: Enrolling kids in Hawaiʻi public schools
entries.summary: Hawaiʻi has one statewide school district (HIDOE). Children attend the home school for the address where they live, and new arrivals need a Hawaiʻi TB clearance, a physical exam done within the past year, immunization records, and proof of address. Students can sometimes start provisionally while health papers are finished.
details: Home school: assigned by your legal address. To attend a different public school you must request a geographic exception.
Proof of address: lease, mortgage or property tax record, or a utility bill in the parent's name. A notarized statement works if you live with family or friends.
Health: a physical exam within one year before first attending a Hawaiʻi school, a TB clearance done in Hawaiʻi, and immunizations by grade. Only medical or religious exemptions are allowed.
Also bring: the child's birth certificate, a parent photo ID, the last report card or transcript, and withdrawal papers from the previous school.
Provisional entry may be allowed with proof of an upcoming medical appointment.
Families in unstable housing can enroll right away; contact the homeless education program at 808-723-4192.

entries.title: Hurricane season prep for new residents
entries.summary: Hurricane season runs June 1 to November 30. Because nearly everything arrives by ship, Hawaiʻi emergency officials ask households to keep at least 14 days of food and water, plus medicine and supplies, and to sign up for county alerts.
details: Season: June 1 to November 30.
Kit: at least 14 days of water (about a gallon per person per day) and food, medications, a battery or crank radio, flashlights, batteries, a first-aid kit, cash, and pet supplies.
Alerts: sign up for your county's alerts (HNL.INFO on Oʻahu; Maui, Hawaiʻi and Kauaʻi counties run their own).
Know if you're in a tsunami evacuation zone (check your county's maps) and where your nearest shelter is.
Before a storm: fill gas tanks, secure lanai furniture, charge phones and power banks.
Renters: get renter's insurance; standard policies may exclude hurricane or flood damage, so ask.

entries.title: Hawaiʻi-only holidays (Kūhiō Day, Kamehameha Day, Statehood Day)
entries.summary: Besides the federal holidays, Hawaiʻi closes state offices and schools for Prince Kūhiō Day (March 26), Good Friday, King Kamehameha Day (June 11) and Statehood Day (the third Friday in August). Lei Day, May 1, isn't an official holiday but is celebrated everywhere.
details: Prince Kūhiō Day, March 26: honors Prince Jonah Kūhiō Kalanianaʻole, who championed the Hawaiian Homes Commission Act. Festivals and hula, especially on Kauaʻi, his birthplace.

Lei Day, May 1: 'May Day is Lei Day in Hawaiʻi.' School May Day programs and lei contests; the big celebration is at Kapiʻolani Park.

entries.title: Where to stay on Oʻahu: areas compared
entries.summary: Most Oʻahu hotels are in Waikīkī, about 25 to 30 minutes from the airport. details: Waikīkī: the most choice at every price, walkable beaches, restaurants and shopping. Parking is expensive, so many visitors skip the rental car. Budget-friendly picks include Wayfinder Waikiki (from about $166 a night).
Kāhala and Diamond Head: quieter, upscale, about 10 minutes past Waikīkī. The Kahala Hotel & Resort is the main hotel.
Ko Olina (West Side): resort lagoons, the Four Seasons and Aulani, about 25 minutes west of the airport. You'll want a car.

North Shore and Lāʻie: The Ritz-Carlton Oʻahu, Turtle Bay is the big resort; Courtyard by Marriott Oʻahu North Shore in Lāʻie is the practical choice near the Polynesian Cultural Center. About an hour from the airport.

Kailua and Lanikai: famous beaches but no resort hotels. Most stays are licensed vacation rentals; Honolulu limits short-term rentals (generally 90 days or more outside resort areas), so book only legal, permitted rentals.
Ala Moana and the marina: The Modern Honolulu (from about $185 a night) and the Prince Waikīkī sit between Waikīkī and Ala Moana Center.

entries.summary: Molokaʻi's only traditional hotel: simple Polynesian-style bungalows on the water just outside Kaunakakai, about 15 minutes from the airport. Expect rustic, old-Hawaiʻi comfort rather than luxury, at about $300 to $350 a night.
details: Area: oceanfront, just east of Kaunakakai town.
From the airport: about 15 minutes by car.
Price: about $300 to $350 a night (early 2026).
Rooms are basic and somewhat dated; there's a pool, hammocks, free parking and laundry.
Hiro's ʻOhana Grill on site is oceanfront. No breakfast is included.
Other options are condos (like Castle Molokaʻi Shores) and vacation rentals; rent a car, because there are no taxis or ride-hail to speak of.
Website: hotelmolokai.com
Rates change by season and demand; check the hotel's own site for current prices and any resort fee.

entries.title: Best time to visit Hawaiʻi (seasons month by month)
entries.summary: Hawaiʻi is warm all year (highs in the low to high 80s °F), so the best time depends on crowds, prices and what you want to do. The sweet spots are late April through May and mid-September through October: dry weather, fewer people and lower rates. Winter (November to April) brings whales and big North Shore surf, and the holidays are the most expensive weeks of the year.
details: Best overall: late April, May, and mid-September through October. May is often the top pick for weather, demand and rates.
Busiest and priciest: Christmas through New Year's, Thanksgiving week, Presidents' Day weekend, spring break and Easter, and July (especially around the Fourth).

Dry season: roughly May to October. Wet season: roughly October to April. Windward and mountain areas (Hilo, Hāna, the North Shore of Kauaʻi) are wetter all year than leeward resort coasts (Waikīkī, Kona, Wailea, Poʻipū).
Whale season: humpbacks are around November through April, with the peak January through March.
Surf: big, dangerous north-shore waves mostly December through February; summer calms the north shores, while south swells hit south-facing beaches.
Hurricane season: June 1 to November 30, with the peak July to September. Storms rarely hit, but watch forecasts and consider travel insurance.
Temperatures (average highs and lows): Honolulu about 81 to 89 °F and 67 to 76 °F; Hilo cooler and much rainier than Kona.
Taxes: the state hotel room tax rose to 11% on Jan. 1, 2026, on top of general excise and county taxes.

entries.title: Ramen in Kailua-Kona
entries.summary: Kona's two go-to ramen shops are Ikkyu Ramen in the Lanihau Center (rated about 4.6 on Google, known for black garlic and curry ramen and big portions) and Daiichi Ramen in Kona Commons (known for its spicy kara and tantanmen ramen, plus katsu and gyoza). Both are open daily for lunch and dinner.
details: Ikkyu Ramen: 75-5595 Palani Road (Lanihau Center), Kailua-Kona. Open daily about 10 a.m. to 9:30 p.m. Phone 808-329-8640. Try the black garlic oil ramen or curry chicken ramen; there's a vegan miso option and katsu plates.

Daiichi Ramen: 74-5452 Makala Boulevard (Kona Commons), Kailua-Kona. Open daily from about 10:30 a.m. into the evening. Known for spicy kara ramen, tantanmen, tonkotsu and black garlic ramen; family-friendly with combo meals and takeout.
Both are a few minutes from Aliʻi Drive and about 15 minutes from the Kona airport.
Hours change; check the shop's listing before you go.

entries.title: Haleʻiwa Joe's (Haleʻiwa and Kāneʻohe)
entries.summary: Haleʻiwa Joe's is a local seafood and grill restaurant with two Oʻahu locations: on the North Shore at 66-011 Kamehameha Highway in Haleʻiwa, by the harbor bridge, and in Kāneʻohe at 46-336 Haʻikū Road, overlooking the pond at Haʻikū Gardens. It's known for fresh fish and a big prime rib.
details: Haleʻiwa (North Shore): 66-011 Kamehameha Highway, Haleʻiwa, by the Anahulu River bridge and the small boat harbor. Phone 808-637-8005. Recent listed hours: lunch and dinner Friday to Sunday from 11 a.m., dinner only Monday to Thursday from 4:30 p.m., closing about 9 p.m.

Kāneʻohe (Haʻikū Gardens): 46-336 Haʻikū Road, Kāneʻohe, in the lush Haʻikū Gardens with a lily pond and mountain views. Phone 808-247-6671. Recent listed hours: dinner nightly from 4:30 p.m. (to 10 p.m. Friday and Saturday), plus Sunday brunch 9 a.m. to 2 p.m.
Known for: fresh island fish (Thai-spiced, macadamia-nut pesto, or steamed with shoyu), and a prime rib that draws a crowd. The two menus differ slightly.
Popular at sunset and on weekends; reservations or an early arrival help, especially in Kāneʻohe.
Hours change; check haleiwajoes.com before you go.
